patterns.what: Apt is currently locked by another process.
patterns.why: Another package manager (like Software Updater or another terminal) is already running or didn't close properly.
patterns.learn: Linux uses lock files to ensure only one process modifies installed packages at a time to prevent corruption.

patterns.what: The command you typed was not found in your system.
patterns.why: Either the package is not installed, or the directory containing it is not in your PATH.
patterns.learn: The PATH variable is a list of directories where the system looks for executable files. If a command is missing, you may need to install it.

patterns.what: The port this application is trying to use is already taken.
patterns.why: Another service or a previous instance of this app is already listening on this port.
patterns.learn: Ports are like doors for network communication. Only one process can use a specific 'door' at a time.

patterns.what: The 'pip' package manager is not installed.
patterns.why: Python is installed, but the pip installer might be missing on some Linux distributions by default.
patterns.learn: Pip is the standard package manager for Python, used to install libraries from the Python Package Index (PyPI).

patterns.what: Python cannot find the library you are trying to use.
patterns.why: The library is either not installed in your current environment or you have a typo in the import name.
patterns.learn: Python uses a search path (sys.path) to locate modules. If a module isn't in one of those folders, it won't be found.

patterns.what: Your disk is full.
patterns.why: A partition or the entire drive has run out of space to write new data.
patterns.learn: Monitoring disk usage is critical. The 'df -h' command shows overall space, while 'du' helps find large files.

patterns.what: There is a merge conflict in your Git repository.
patterns.why: Someone else made changes to the same part of a file you're working on.
patterns.learn: Git conflicts occur when two branches have diametrically opposed changes that Git can't resolve automatically.

match: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by merge
patterns.what: You have unstaged changes that Git refuses to overwrite.
patterns.why: Pulling new code would delete your local work because it's not committed or stashed.

fix.default: git stash && git pull && git stash pop

patterns.learn: Stashing is a great way to 'pause' your work and save it for later without making a commit.

match: Cannot connect to the Docker daemon
patterns.what: The Docker daemon is not running.
patterns.why: Docker service needs to be started to run containers.
patterns.learn: Docker runs as a background service (daemon) that manages containers on your system.

patterns.what: SSH authentication failed.
patterns.why: The server doesn't recognize your SSH key or you haven't specified the right identity file.
patterns.learn: SSH keys use asymmetric cryptography to provide secure, passwordless authentication.

patterns.what: Your system cannot resolve the website's address (DNS).
patterns.why: You might be offline, or your DNS settings are incorrect.
patterns.learn: DNS is like a phonebook for the internet, translating names like 'google.com' into IP addresses.

patterns.what: You're trying to remove a directory that still has files inside.
patterns.why: The standard 'rmdir' command only works on empty folders.
patterns.learn: The '-r' (recursive) flag tells 'rm' to delete a folder and everything inside it.

patterns.what: The connection was rejected by the server.
patterns.why: Either the server is down, or no service is listening on that specific port.
patterns.learn: A 'refused' connection means the system actually reached the host, but the port was closed.

patterns.what: You're trying to perform a file operation on a folder.
patterns.why: The command expected a single file, but you provided a directory path.
patterns.learn: In Linux, everything is a file, but directories and regular files are treated differently by most tools.

patterns.what: You're trying to access a file as if it were a folder.
patterns.why: A component of the path prefix is not a directory.
patterns.learn: This often happens when a file has the same name as a directory you're trying to create or access.

patterns.what: The program crashed due to a memory access violation.
patterns.why: Requested memory that doesn't belong to it, often due to a bug in the code (C/C++, etc.).
patterns.learn: Segmentation faults occur when a process tries to access a restricted memory area.

patterns.what: There is a structural error in your Python code.
patterns.why: You have a typo, missing colon, or incorrect indentation.
patterns.learn: Python is very strict about white space and syntax rules to ensure readability.

patterns.what: Node Package Manager (npm) error or not found.
patterns.why: Either npm is not installed, or you have a networking/DNS issue while installing packages.
patterns.learn: NPM is the default package manager for Node.js, managing millions of available Javascript libraries.

patterns.what: You're trying to write to a drive that is locked for writing.
patterns.why: The filesystem was mounted as read-only, often due to an error during boot or hardware failure.
patterns.learn: Linux mounts filesystems as read-only if it detects corruption to prevent further data loss.

patterns.what: The system blocked this operation.
patterns.why: Unlike 'Permission denied', this usually means the operation is not allowed even for root (e.g., immutable files).
patterns.learn: File attributes like 'immutable' or 'append-only' can block operations regardless of user permissions.

patterns.what: Python's global environment is locked on this system.
patterns.why: Modern Linux distros (Debian 12+, Ubuntu 23.04+) prevent 'pip' from modified system libraries to avoid breaking the OS.
patterns.learn: PEP 668 introduced this to ensure system stability. Use Virtual Environments (venv) or 'pipx' for isolated applications.

match: E: Could not open lock file
E: Unable to acquire the dpkg frontend lock
patterns.what: You don't have the necessary permissions for this command.
patterns.why: This command requires administrative (root) privileges to modify system files.
patterns.learn: 'sudo' (superuser do) allows you to run commands with root privileges. Using it carefully is essential for system security.
